description: We are building the "Agricultural Adaptation System," a tool designed to help farmers decide what to plant and when, adapting to climate shifts using NASA POWER data
summary:
Mosim – موسم
Mosim is an Arabic-first, bilingual agricultural decision-support pilot for rainfed wheat rotations in Rabba, Al-Karak, Jordan, where rainfall is scarce and erratic. A farmer choosing the next crop must connect the crop’s purpose, local research, rainfall, regional soil moisture and field conditions, yet these sources use different dates, scales and units. Mosim brings reviewed local rotation research together with NASA POWER weather and SMAP soil-moisture data, FAO/IIASA land-suitability information and Copernicus Sentinel-2 imagery, and answers three plain-language questions: which crop to consider, why, and what to check before planting. For the supported Rabba wheat scenario, a grain-sale goal highlights lentil and a forage goal highlights vetch. Where local evidence does not apply, Mosim withholds a recommendation instead of making an unsupported claim. Every source keeps its date, scale, units and completeness visible, and a missing reading is never shown as dry soil. Mosim turns Earth-observation data into a clearer planting conversation; yield gains, profit and water savings have not been measured.
details:
What it does: Gives a farmer an option to consider, a local evidence-based reason, and one practical pre-planting field check, in Arabic and English. Detailed crop comparisons, maps, charts and source information remain available under “See the data and details”.
How it works: The farmer opens the public Rabba demo or enters a custom pin, previous crop, usual next crop, water regime, goal and an optional field boundary. Backend rules apply the reviewed Rabba evidence (grain sale highlights lentil, forage highlights vetch, and no crop is recommended for unsupported locations or conditions). Mosim then loads dated NASA POWER, NASA SMAP, Sentinel-2 and GAEZ records with their units, spatial scale and completeness, and shows a built-in explanation first.
Benefits: Makes evidence easier to interpret, gives direct access to original sources, and clearly flags unavailable or pending data instead of turning it into a dry-soil warning.
What we hope to achieve: A clearer conversation before seed purchase, without promising yield, profit or planting results.
Limits: Weather and satellite indicators describe the region, not the farmer’s own soil. The pilot covers Rabba only, and field outcomes, yield gains and water savings have not been measured.
Validation: 81 automated unit, API and provider tests and type checks passed at the last recorded step. Screenshots cover grain-sale, forage, unsupported-location, pending-SMAP, missing-data and mobile cases using saved, verified public data and clearly labeled controlled failure tests.
Tools and software: React and Vite (bilingual interface), Express and TypeScript (APIs and decision rules), PostgreSQL (backend storage), Playwright (automated browser testing and screenshots), NASA Earthdata AppEEARS and Copernicus Data Space / Sentinel Hub (data access), and optional OpenRouter wording restricted to backend-approved facts and actions.
projectRefs: Local Jordanian crop-rotation trials in Rabba
